title: Bereavement support and organ donation
blurb: Support families around a death and apply UK opt-out organ donation law, including when to involve the specialist nurse.
question: Callum, 29, is on an intensive care unit in England after a catastrophic brain injury. His GCS is 3 without sedation and the team are discussing whether brainstem death tests are appropriate. His mother asks the bedside nurse, 'Does he have to be a donor now the law has changed?' What should happen?

teach.body: Good end of life care does not stop at the moment of death. It includes supporting the family and others important to the person (the 'key contacts') through the death and into bereavement, respecting spiritual, religious and cultural wishes, and making organ and tissue donation possible where the person wanted it. Supporting families is one of the five Priorities for Care of the Dying Person.
teach.cite: Hospice UK Care after death 5.2 (2025); Priorities for Care (2014)

teach.h: Supporting the bereaved at the time of death
items: Offer all key contacts the chance to view the person; even after traumatic deaths many find this helpful.
Offer them the chance to take part in care after death, such as washing, if they wish.
Respect spiritual, religious and cultural wishes; involve chaplaincy or faith representatives where wanted.
Offer mementoes such as a lock of hair or handprints.
Give clear information on what happens next: the bereavement office in hospital, the GP surgery in the community.
Guide them on supporting bereaved children and young people.

teach.h: Who to point families to next
head: Place of death
First contact for next steps
teach.caption: Hospice UK Care after death 5.2 para 33: these services know the local bereavement agencies that can support key contacts.

teach.body: In care homes and other communal settings, other residents may have close relationships with the person who died and need to be told. Do this compassionately and sensitively, using accessible resources where needed (for example for people with learning disabilities), but without giving information about the cause or reason for death. Consider signposting them to bereavement support.
teach.cite: Hospice UK Care after death 5.2 para 44

teach.h: Opt-out organ donation across the UK
teach.caption: All UK nations and the Crown Dependencies (Jersey, Guernsey, Isle of Man) now have opt-out systems (NHS Blood and Transplant).

teach.h: Opt-out in England: who is excluded?

root.label: Adult dies where donation is possible

children.label: Deemed consent does not apply
children.sub: under 18; lacked capacity for a long period; visitor or not living here voluntarily; lived in England < 12 months

teach.caption: In an opt-out system people still choose: they can register a decision to donate or not on the NHS Organ Donor Register at any time.

teach.h: Identify, refer, let the specialist nurse lead
teach.body: NICE CG135 asks teams to identify potential donors early: after catastrophic brain injury, the absence of one or more cranial nerve reflexes and a GCS of 4 or less not explained by sedation, or a plan to withdraw life-sustaining treatment expected to lead to circulatory death. At that point, start discussions with the specialist nurse for organ donation (SNOD). The approach to the family is planned by a multidisciplinary team, including the SNOD, and made privately and compassionately, at a time that suits them.

rows.label: Example
values: Corneas: up to 24 h after death

teach.caption: Hospice UK 5.2 para 12. Closing the eyes with light pressure also protects corneas for donation.

teach.body: Callum, 29, has lost several cranial nerve reflexes and has a GCS of 3 not explained by sedation, which meets the NICE trigger, so his nurse Precious tells the consultant and the SNOD is contacted. When his mother asks about the law, Precious explains gently that the specialist nurse will talk the family through Callum's wishes and the choices, and that families are always consulted. The SNOD checks the Organ Donor Register; Callum had registered to donate. The family are supported to spend time with him and the chaplain visits at their request.

teach.text: Opt-out does not mean families are bypassed: in England the family is still consulted. And don't raise organ donation with the family yourself without a plan: identify and refer to the SNOD, who leads the planned MDT approach. Don't confuse organ donation (organised before death in ICU or ED) with tissue donation (possible after death, corneas up to 24 hours).

items: Offer viewing, involvement in care, mementoes and clear next-step information.
Inform residents in communal settings sensitively, without the cause of death.
All UK nations have opt-out: England 20 May 2020, Scotland 26 March 2021 (deemed authorisation), NI 1 June 2023, Wales December 2015.
England exclusions: under 18, lacked capacity for a significant period, visitors or not resident voluntarily, lived in England < 12 months.
Families are still consulted; the SNOD leads a planned approach.
Refer when one or more cranial nerve reflexes are absent and GCS ≤ 4 not due to sedation, or when withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment is planned.

summary: You can now support bereaved families and other residents at and after a death and point families to the right next steps. You can also apply UK opt-out organ donation law, recognise when to refer to the specialist nurse for organ donation and tell organ donation apart from tissue donation.

A.q: On what date did the opt-out (deemed consent) system for organ donation come into effect in England?
options: 1 December 2015
26 March 2021
1 June 2023
A.why: NHS Blood and Transplant: the opt-out system in England began on 20 May 2020.

whyNot.0: December 2015 is when Wales introduced deemed consent.
whyNot.2: 26 March 2021 is the Scottish date (deemed authorisation).
whyNot.3: 1 June 2023 is the Northern Ireland date.

A.q: Which person in England is in an excluded group, so deemed consent for organ donation does not apply?
options: A 45-year-old who has not registered any decision
A 30-year-old who moved to England 8 months ago
A 70-year-old who registered to donate
A 19-year-old who has lived in England all his life
A.why: England's excluded groups include people who have lived in England for less than 12 months before their death.

whyNot.0: Not registering a decision is exactly when deemed consent can apply.
whyNot.2: This person has expressly consented by registering.
whyNot.3: Adults over 18 who have lived in England for over 12 months are not excluded.

A.q: A man dies on a medical ward. His wife asks if his corneas can still be donated, as he wished. What is accurate?
options: Cornea donation is possible up to 24 hours after death
Cornea donation must be organised before death in ICU
Cornea donation is not possible after a ward death
Cornea donation must take place within 2 hours of death
A.why: Hospice UK 5.2: tissue donation is possible after death; cornea donation can happen up to 24 hours after death, in hospitals, hospices and funeral homes.

whyNot.1: Organising before death applies to organ donation in ICU and ED, not to corneas.
whyNot.2: Corneas can be donated after a death on a ward.
whyNot.3: The window is up to 24 hours, not 2 hours.

B.q: Mr Tan, 61, is ventilated on ICU after a massive stroke. At a family meeting the consultant agrees that life-sustaining treatment will be withdrawn tomorrow. A staff nurse wonders whether he could donate his kidneys. What is the next step?
options: The nurse asks the family what Mr Tan would have wanted
Treatment is withdrawn first, and donation is discussed later
The nurse checks the Organ Donor Register herself
The team contact the specialist nurse for organ donation
B.why: NICE CG135 1.1.2–1.1.3: a plan to withdraw life-sustaining treatment is a trigger; the team should start discussions with the specialist nurse for organ donation at that point. The family approach is then planned by the MDT including the SNOD.

whyNot.0: An unplanned approach by one nurse is not recommended; the MDT plans the approach with the SNOD.
whyNot.1: Organ donation must be organised before withdrawal; delaying the referral removes the option.
whyNot.2: Register checks are part of the SNOD-led process.

B.q: At lunch in a residential home, Mrs Pryce asks the nurse why her neighbour Edna's door is shut and her name has gone from the door. Edna died last night. What is the best response?
options: Tell Mrs Pryce that Edna has gone into hospital
Explain in full how Edna died so that she understands
Say it is confidential and gently change the subject
Tell her gently that Edna has died, without the cause
B.why: Hospice UK 5.2 para 44: residents in communal settings often need to know of a death; inform them sensitively, without giving information about the cause or reason for death, and consider bereavement support.

whyNot.0: A false account is dishonest and will add to Mrs Pryce's distress later.
whyNot.1: Details of the cause of death are confidential and should not be shared.
whyNot.2: Confidentiality does not prevent telling a fellow resident that a death has occurred.

B.q: Mr Hall has died on a surgical ward. His daughter arrives and asks the nurse whether it would be 'a good idea' to go in and see him, because she is frightened of what he will look like. What should the nurse do?
options: Offer viewing and prepare her for what she will see
Advise her not to view, to protect her memories
Tell her viewing takes place at the funeral director's
Ask the doctor to decide whether viewing is suitable
B.why: Hospice UK 5.2: all key contacts should be offered the chance to view the person; there is evidence that even after traumatic deaths many find it helpful. Preparing her supports her choice.

whyNot.1: Discouraging viewing removes her choice and is not supported by the evidence.
whyNot.2: Viewing can take place in hospital as well as later at the funeral director's.
whyNot.3: This is her choice, supported by the nurse, not a medical decision.

C.q: Rhian, 52, was injured in a road collision and is on ICU in England. She moved from Cardiff to Leeds 20 years ago, had capacity and never recorded a donation decision. Death is confirmed by brainstem tests. Her husband says they never discussed donation. Which statement is accurate?
options: Donation cannot proceed, as she did not register to donate
Her husband's agreement is irrelevant once deemed consent applies
Deemed consent may apply, and her husband is still consulted
Deemed consent does not apply as she was born in Wales
C.why: Rhian is over 18, not in an excluded group and did not opt out, so deemed consent may apply. NHSBT: families are still consulted if donation is a possibility, and the SNOD leads that conversation.

whyNot.0: Under opt-out, not registering does not prevent donation.
whyNot.1: Families are always consulted, even in an opt-out system.
whyNot.3: The English exclusion depends on having lived in England for less than 12 months before death, not on place of birth; Rhian has lived in Leeds for 20 years.

C.q: A nurse on ICU recognises a possible organ donor. Which group does NICE CG135 say should plan and make the approach to the family?
options: The bedside nurse caring for the patient
The patient's GP, who knows the family
A multidisciplinary team including the SNOD
The hospital chaplain with the family's faith leader
C.why: NICE CG135 1.1.11–1.1.12: an MDT, led by an identifiable consultant and including the specialist nurse for organ donation (and faith representatives where relevant), plans the approach.

whyNot.0: A single nurse acting alone is not the planned MDT approach.
whyNot.1: The GP is not part of the planned ICU approach.
whyNot.3: Faith representatives may be included where relevant, but do not lead the approach.

C.q: Mrs Okeke dies at home. Her son asks the district nurse, 'What do we do now? Who do we call?' Who should the nurse direct him to for the next steps?
options: The local registrar's office
The GP surgery
The hospital bereavement office
The coroner's office
C.why: Hospice UK 5.2 para 33: after a death in the community, the key contact is usually directed to the GP surgery for the next steps, and the surgery knows local bereavement agencies.

whyNot.0: Registration is booked later, once the medical certificate is completed.
whyNot.2: The bereavement office is the contact for deaths in hospital.
whyNot.3: The coroner is involved only if referral criteria are met.

reteach.title: Two jobs at one bedside
reteach.question: At the death of a possible donor, what are the nurse's two jobs?

blocks.h: Comfort the family, connect the specialist
blocks.body: Job one is the family: time, privacy, honest information, viewing, faith needs and clear next steps. Job two is to recognise the donation trigger (absent cranial nerve reflexes with GCS 4 or less not due to sedation, or a plan to withdraw treatment) and connect the team with the specialist nurse for organ donation, who leads a planned approach. The law (opt-out) changes the starting assumption, not the need to talk with the family.

blocks.text: Scotland's term is deemed AUTHORISATION; England and Wales use deemed CONSENT.

explain.body: Offer viewing, participation in care, mementoes, and faith or chaplaincy support. Give next-step information: bereavement office in hospital, GP surgery in the community.

test.q: Which item may be offered to a family as a memento during care after death?
options: A lock of hair
The medical notes
The syringe pump
The death certificate draft
test.why: Hospice UK 5.2 para 46: mementoes such as locks of hair or handprints may be offered.

whyNot.1: Medical notes are confidential records, not mementoes.
whyNot.2: Equipment is cleaned or disposed of per policy.
whyNot.3: The certificate is a legal document completed by a doctor, not a memento.

explain.body: All UK nations have opt-out. England 20 May 2020 and Wales December 2015 (deemed consent); Scotland 26 March 2021 (deemed authorisation); Northern Ireland 1 June 2023. People can still record a decision on the NHS Organ Donor Register.

test.q: What term describes Scotland's opt-out organ donation law?
options: Deemed consent
Deemed authorisation
Presumed agreement
Implied permission to donate
test.why: NHSBT: 'deemed authorisation' is the name for the organ donation law in Scotland.

whyNot.0: Deemed consent is the term in England and Wales.
whyNot.2: This is not the statutory term used in Scotland.
whyNot.3: This is not a term used in UK organ donation law.

explain.body: Deemed consent does not apply to under-18s, people who lacked capacity to understand the arrangements for a significant period, visitors and those not living in England voluntarily, or people who lived in England less than 12 months before death.

test.q: Which person would NOT be covered by deemed consent in England?
options: A 17-year-old who has not registered a decision
A 25-year-old who has not registered a decision
A 45-year-old who has lived in England for 5 years
An 80-year-old with no recorded decision
test.why: People under 18 are an excluded group in England.

whyNot.1: An adult who has not opted out and is not excluded may be covered by deemed consent.
whyNot.2: Five years of residence exceeds the 12-month threshold, so this adult is not excluded.
whyNot.3: Older age is not an exclusion.

explain.body: NICE CG135: after catastrophic brain injury, absence of one or more cranial nerve reflexes and GCS 4 or less not explained by sedation, or a plan to withdraw life-sustaining treatment expected to lead to circulatory death. Then contact the SNOD.

test.q: After a catastrophic brain injury, what GCS score not explained by sedation is a NICE CG135 trigger to discuss organ donation with the SNOD?
options: 8 or less
6 or less
4 or less
test.why: NICE CG135 1.1.2: a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 4 or less that is not explained by sedation, together with the absence of one or more cranial nerve reflexes.

whyNot.0: A GCS of 8 or less is a common airway threshold, not the donation trigger.
whyNot.1: Six is not the CG135 threshold.
whyNot.3: A GCS of 3 is included, but the trigger is 4 or less, so patients scoring 4 would be missed.
